sources.headline: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
sources.text: The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives.""These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.

sources.headline: Food suppliers in UK hit by cyber-attacks after freezers targeted in Europe
sources.text:
Food suppliers in the UK have been hit by cyber-attacks after hackers raised the temperatures of supermarket freezers across Europe.The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NSCS) said it was working with the affected companies but the national impact was minimal.Speaking at the launch of the NCSC’s annual review on Tuesday, its director of operations, Paul Chichester, said: “We’re aware of those incidents in the UK, and obviously we’re working with the affected organisations. We’ll keep monitoring that. At the moment, the impact is minimal.”Cybersecurity experts meanwhile reported that attacks on “dummy” fridge controls – deliberately placed online to lure would-be hackers – displayed characteristics similar to malicious operations linked to Russia.Cold war? Why are fridges being hacked and what could be next? - The LatestRetailers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday – with some rising to as high as 50C (122F) – and several companies confirming they had been hacked.Similar incidents were reported in France last month. It has emerged that the cyber-attack on French supermarket fridges involved legacy technology connected to the internet with default passwords.No UK grocery chain has been directly affected so far.Chichester said the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was working with organisations to identify loopholes in their technology and close them before hackers exploited them.‘It’s a form of terrorism’: fridges across Europe hit by suspected cyber-attacks – videoHe said the NCSC was not able to comment on who might have carried out the attacks, but that they were not AI-enabled and had used vulnerabilities that had been “out there for a long period of time”.The NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, said the fridge attacks represented the “foothills” of an enlarged cyberthreat that companies and the public faced as AI systems highlighted flaws in IT networks that owners were not aware of or had neglected to patch.“There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited,” he added.The agency’s chief technology officer, Ollie Whitehouse, said everyday domestic devices connected to the internet would be susceptible to hackers in certain situations. He said manufacturers needed to be encouraged to make their technology safer, and consumers needed to accept paying more for safer equipment.The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers said some of its more than 300 members had been affected after becoming “collateral” in the hack.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionThe industry body said no meat had been lost in the refrigeration hacks but the incidents were a “reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets”.One meat supply company saw its cold units rise to up to 100C while another two reported their units had started to defrost. The association said the affected units were empty at the time.A fruit and vegetable wholesaler in London was also affected but prevented the attack from escalating by pulling the internet connection to its cold storage units out at the wall.Alex Pearce, managing director of Langridge Organic, said the hackers had changed the parameters on a number of units, setting them to defrost for more than four hours at 150C. However, Pearce and his staff intervened before any stock could be damaged.“It clearly must have been easy to get in [to the system] because the simple solution was to unplug ourselves from the internet,” he said.Pearce said Langridge uses the same fridge control system, developed by a US software company called Copeland, that was involved in the French supermarket incidents. The Grocer news website first reported the Langridge incident. Copeland said it is talking to affected customers and has recommended software fixes.Cybersecurity researchers said attacks on dummy Danfoss fridge controls – whose systems were also targeted by the hackers in mainland Europe – were similar to recent operations linked to Russia.
Xavier Bellekens, the chief executive of the cyberdefence firm Lupovis, said it had recorded 256 attempted attacks from 91 different sources between 20 October and 30 October after setting up online “honeypot” traps that are indistinguishable to attackers from real Danfoss fridge controllers.
The attackers attempting to take over the dummy controls remained anonymous, but most of the authentication attempts used the manufacturer’s publicly documented factory-default username and password credentials.They also used what Bellekens called “bulletproof” hosting, which means using internet service providers that are particularly tolerant of malicious activity, often ignore abuse complaints or make it difficult for authorities to disrupt their customers’ operations.
“What caught our attention was the overlap between infrastructure involved in the recent probing activity and infrastructure we have previously associated with Russian-linked malicious operations,” he said.“While we are not able to pinpoint a group yet, the number of actors that fit this bill is relatively small and the bulletproof hosting we have seen being used by these actors for probing was also being used by Russian groups some time ago.”

sources.headline: Italy holds emergency talks as supermarket fridge attacks spread across Europe
sources.text:
Published on
3 November 2026 - 21:22 GMT+1
Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence chiefs on Tuesday after cyberattacks on supermarket freezer systems hit at least 11 European countries in recent days.
Supermarkets in at least 10 EU countries, including Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, have been forced to throw away food after temperatures rose in their fridges and freezers. The UK has also been affected.
Nobody has claimed responsibility and the motive remains unknown.
The Italian government said the impact so far was “highly limited”, and that only outlets with outdated security systems had been affected. Around 20 stores were reported hit nationwide.
Ministers nevertheless met intelligence chiefs and Italy’s National Cyber Security Agency, which issued technical advice to retailers on protecting their systems.
Giuseppe Spadaro, director of a group that runs Coop supermarkets in Sicily, said four of its 300 stores had been hit. “We had to throw away everything. The shelves are empty,” he told the Corriere della Sera newspaper.
EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said EU agencies were working with national authorities on a collective response. “These are not isolated incidents, and of course, we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said.
On Monday, EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen called the attacks a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain”.
Romania’s cybersecurity chief took a different view. Six Romanian outlets were affected, but Dan Cimpean, director of the country’s National Cyber Security Directorate, said: “It seems semi-amateurish. We do not suspect, under any circumstances, that it is a state actor.”
In the UK, National Cyber Security Centre chief Richard Horne told the BBC the issue affected “the whole food supply chain”, and that there had been a couple of instances where “vulnerable technology had been exploited”.
Four stores were hit in Germany. In Sweden, the Coop chain said its seven affected shops were back to normal, and that the equipment involved had been connected over old 4G mobile networks.
Belgium was among the hardest-hit countries, and federal prosecutors there have opened an investigation. Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit by a similar attack last month.
Supermarket refrigeration systems are often connected to the internet so that contractors can monitor and repair them remotely. Recent research by the security firm Forescout found nearly 13,000 refrigeration control services openly reachable online in 99 countries

sources.text: Cyber hackers have targeted fridges and freezers in supermarkets in several European countries including Ireland – causing temperatures to increase and food to spoil.

sources.headline: More European grocery stores hit by apparent fridge-freezer hacks
sources.text:
Updated on: November 2, 2026 / 8:51 PM EST
/ CBS/AFP
Add CBS News on Google
Grocery store chains in at least three European countries reported unexpected temperature spikes Monday in refrigerators and freezers that ruined food — the second time in less than a month that similar incidents have raised concerns about cyberattacks on increasingly interlinked infrastructure.Netherlands-based food retailer Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium both said an IT incident overnight had sent temperatures inside fridges and freezers in dozens of their stores in Belgium and Luxembourg soaring, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar spikes, with one outlet explicitly blaming a cyberattack, according to the Reuters news agency.The incidents come less than three weeks after several French supermarket chains said they were hit by a cyberattack that sent refrigerator temperatures surging as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit in hundreds of outlets.French chains E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U told the AFP news agency last month that they had suffered a cyberattack. On Monday, Reuters said Ahold, the Dutch grocery store chain, had reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands in October after detecting suspicious activity in its infrastructure. The chain realized there were temperature increases in the cooling systems on Monday, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester told Reuters. The CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates the systems used by Delhaize and other chains, told Belgium's national Belga news agency a cyberattack was to blame after fridge and freezer units' evaporators were switched into defrost mode."We began mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control," Stephan Moelans told Belga. "We've been working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network."
"Over the past few weeks, we've been working very hard to protect our customers' fridges against this vulnerability," he told the news agency, but he added that many units would require physical modifications, and "that requires investment."
An employee cleans freezers that lost power at an ICA supermarket in Stockholm on Nov. 2, 2026, after a number of stores suffered problems with their refrigerators and freezers overnight.
Fredrik SANDBERG/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP/Getty
A handful of Swedish supermarkets also saw refrigerator and freezer temperatures soar early Monday, two chains said, forcing them to throw away spoiled food. ICA and Coop both told AFP they had no immediate information about their systems being subjected to a cyberattack.ICA told AFP "a limited number" of its stores were affected, but it did not provide a number. One of its stores, in Sjobo in southern Sweden, posted on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had "been hacked and they set the temperature at 50 degrees" Celsius (about 122 degrees Fahrenheit)."We are looking into what has happened and the scale of it," spokesperson Helena Johansson told AFP, adding that the company was focusing on how to help affected stores.
Employees throw away bags of spoiled food outside an ICA supermarket on in Stockholm, Nov. 2, 2026.
Fredrik SANDBERG/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP/Getty
The Coop chain said six of its around 800 stores in Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers and had to throw out food, with company spokesman Carlos Cancino telling AFP that the units "either stopped working entirely or have been partially impaired."
"I haven't received any information that this is a cyberattack," he said.On Oct. 12, major French retailers said hundreds of stores were hit by a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems, which forced them to throw out food and raised concerns about food security. In that incident, refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
View of the closed frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes, France, after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems, causing food losses and fires at several stores, on Oct. 12, 2026.
Stephane Mahe/REUTERS
There has been no claim of responsibility for any hack targeting grocery retailers in Europe to date.Speaking after the French stores were forced to discard thousands of pounds of wasted food last month due to the still-unattributed hack, European Union food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said in a post on X that "food security requires more attention at all levels," calling the "exploitation" of vulnerabilities in such essential, networked systems a new "reality." "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher wrote on X last month.Prosecutors in Paris confirmed a cyberattack and said it also hit other major chains and sparked fires as some equipment overheated.

sources.headline: European supermarkets rush to patch vulnerabilities after region-wide fridge hack
sources.text: COPENHAGEN/LONDON - European supermarkets targeted in a second wave of cyberattacks that cranked up fridge and freezer temperatures were rushing on Nov 3 to upgrade their systems and protect themselves against further hacking attempts.Stores in eight European countries were forced to throw away vast quantities of food after hackers tampered on Nov 2 with their fridges, in an attack identical to one that swept dozens of supermarkets in France three weeks ago.In Sweden, supermarket chain Coop said it was switching systems to 5G networks and modern modems, instead of 4G connections - a process that had already started since the French incident.The seven stores hit by the attack are back up and running, but their refrigeration systems have been disconnected from the internet, a spokesperson said.“We are looking quite thoroughly and deeply into the status of the entire network of stores to see if we risk any vulnerability anywhere in the entire network,” the spokesperson added.Software provider Danfoss, whose systems were again among those targeted, said it has been in close contact with customers over the past three weeks to help them manage the situation, and recommended that systems should not be directly accessible via the internet.“Retailers need to act now. They should identify whether their refrigerator controllers are vulnerable, check if they are connected to the internet, ensure they’ve got the latest security updates and are supported by the manufacturer. And if they don’t even know, then remove them from the public internet immediately,” said Frank Groenewegen, cybersecurity expert at Deloitte in The Hague.“With disconnecting, you haven’t fixed the root cause, but you’ve at least isolated those systems so that an attacker is not able to do this anymore.”‘Heightened alert’Many European supermarkets are run by independent business owners in a cooperative structure, meaning systems are not the same across stores.Swedish grocer ICA said all 23 stores hit in the Nov 2 cyberattack had equipment connected outside the chain’s centrally managed store network.ICA store owner Christian Olofsson said he felt even more frustrated about the cyberattack given he was in the process of changing the security systems at his stores in Tomelilla and Sjobo in Sweden when they were hacked.A Swedish police spokesperson said around 10 police reports had been filed since Nov 2, and they expected more.Ireland's third-largest supermarket chain, SuperValu, said on Nov 2 that refrigeration systems limited to a specific model in 13 of its 223 stores were affected by a cyber incident, with chilled and frozen products removed from sale. PHOTO: REUTERSGerman supermarket operator Edeka, which had fridges hacked at a store in Reisbach, Germany, told Reuters there are no standardised refrigeration systems across its network of stores run by independent retailers.Even integrated supermarket groups were not immune: Carrefour, which had 80 franchised stores in France hacked three weeks ago, suffered the same cyberattack again at 15 stores in Belgium on Nov 2.EU cybersecurity agency ENISA said the large-scale nature of the cyberattacks targeting retail across several member states “underscores the importance of European cooperation, rapid information-sharing and coordinated responses to cyber incidents”.In Britain, hackers tried to target small meat-processing firms, but the impact was minimal, said Richard Horne, chief executive of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).The NCSC is working with organisations to spot vulnerabilities and close them before somebody exploits them, Horne said. "We're obviously on heightened alert."The attack on supermarket fridges is just an early sign of what are likely to be increasingly frequent disruptions as old technology fails to keep pace with hackers, Horne said. REUTERS

A spate of appliance malfunctions at U.S. military facilities over the summer seemed like just a nuisance: Refrigeration systems had failed at commissaries, spoiling food and temporarily limiting supplies.

Then, last month, freezers malfunctioned at hundreds of grocery stores in France in what officials called a cyberattack. On Monday, retailers in at least seven more European countries reported problems with refrigeration units.

Though it was not clear what caused the disruptions, experts said they had the hallmarks of cyberattacks. On Monday, the U.S. Army said that its cyber investigators were looking into the issue.

Here’s what to know:

What happened at the U.S. military sites?

On Aug. 26, freezers at a market in Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona, suddenly went into defrost mode, according to a Facebook post from the base. All the food in those freezers was spoiled.

ADVERTISEMENT

The same day, Naval Station Newport in Newport, R.I., reported “refrigeration system issues at the commissary.”

Army officials are now investigating whether those malfunctions and others at U.S. military facilities in August were part of a wider cyberattack, Reuters reported last week. Asked on Monday about the Reuters report, the Pentagon acknowledged “speculation regarding a potential cyber incident” and said that its inspector general’s office was investigating the matter.

Published: 10:18pm, 2 Nov 2026Updated: 11:24am, 3 Nov 2026

A suspected cyberattack hit grocery stores across at least nine European countries on Monday, prompting the EU to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the bloc’s food supply chain.

Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden reported refrigeration problems that forced some retailers to discard food after temperatures rose overnight.

The incident came three weeks after a cyberattack disrupted French grocery stores and forced hundreds of outlets to throw away spoiled stock.

While no one has claimed responsibility for either attack, the incidents have heightened concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure amid growing security tensions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations.

EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc was taking the incidents “very seriously”.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously,” he said.

Frozen goods being thrown away at ICA Kvantum in Sjobo, Sweden. Photo: EPA

In Italy, at least four Coop supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to media reports and the national cybersecurity agency.

The Italian government was to hold a cybersecurity meeting with intelligence services on Tuesday.

“The attack happened at 4am (0300 GMT),” Giuseppe Spadaro, head of the Radenza Group which manages Coop-branded supermarkets, told Italian news agency ANSA.

The attack targeted “our remote-control system for frozen food sections” and had since been resolved, he added.

Belgium was among the hardest-hit countries, with dozens of stores across several grocery chains reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors opened an investigation.

“It’s a cyberattack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a spokesman for Carrefour Belgium, which reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 stores.

Empty refrigerators in a Delhaize supermarket in Boortmeerbeek, some 30km from Brussels. Photo: AFP

Ikea said its Mons outlet also experienced a cyberattack that caused freezer temperatures to rise.

Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel said it had begun securing its installations after the October attack in France, but some systems had yet to be upgraded and were among those affected on Monday.

Delhaize, Colruyt and Intermarche also reported refrigeration problems at stores in Belgium, while four Delhaize outlets in Luxembourg were affected.

In Ireland, retailer Musgrave said 13 Supervalu stores were impacted by what it described as a cyber incident.

A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruptions.

In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group confirmed incidents at seven Intermarche stores linked to a cyberattack, which “appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems”.

In Sweden, Coop confirmed six of its around 800 stores had been hit.

“We can confirm that it is a cyber incident. The problem has now been resolved and the fridges and freezers are working as normal,” spokesman Carlos Cancino said.

He said Coop did not know who was behind the attack, but noted that the affected stores had been connected to a 4G mobile network, not the updated 5G system, which made them “more exposed” to hackers.

Swedish chain Ica also said “a limited number” of its stores experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyberattack.

According to Ica spokesperson Helena Johansson, the affected stores were all connected to an external refrigeration control system provided by Danish manufacturer Danfoss – the same supplier targeted in the October 12 cyberattack on French retailers. She referred all queries to Danfoss.

In Finland, irregular temperatures were also detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group.

“We are currently investigating the cause, and interference via the network has not yet been ruled out,” Petri Kayhko, head of Kesko’s corporate security, said.

Roni Kokkola, an information security specialist at the National Cyber Security Centre at Finland’s Transport and Communications Agency Traficom, would not rule out cyber interference.

“We’ve seen this in Europe in the past few months, so it spreading beyond France to other countries has been expected,” he said.

“Nowadays, it’s very typical that all kinds of vulnerabilities are being exploited ever more actively and rapidly.”

In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50 degrees Celsius, public broadcaster ERR reported.

The units were older models delivered by Danfoss, similar to the ones targeted in the France attack, Jann Mutso, director of Kitman Coldtech, a manufacturer and distributor of advanced refrigeration systems, told ERR.
